title: Germany's Twin Crisis: Political Fractures and an Economic Recovery That Households Cannot Yet Feel
excerpt: Germany's governing coalition is struggling to contain the electoral rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland while simultaneously trying to convince voters that a genuine economic recovery is underway. The two crises are deeply intertwined: political instability is undermining confidence in democratic government at precisely the moment when citizens most need competent economic management. For Europe's largest economy, the stakes extend well beyond Berlin.
body:
The Firewall Under Pressure

The election of an AfD politician as president of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament, secured with votes from parties across the spectrum, has sharpened debate about whether Germany's mainstream parties can hold their informal agreement not to cooperate with the far right. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has publicly warned that extremism is entering Germany's legislatures and has urged other parties to stand firm. Yet the Saxony-Anhalt episode exposed how secret ballots and shifting parliamentary alliances can erode that commitment under practical pressure.

The AfD's growing institutional presence rests on a platform that combines opposition to mass immigration, hostility to sanctions against Russia, criticism of Germany's energy transition and claims that established parties have lost touch with ordinary citizens. In eastern Germany in particular, the party has become the largest force in several state legislatures. Its rise is not uniform in its motivations: electoral data does not establish that all AfD voters endorse every element of its programme, but it does reflect deep dissatisfaction with the alternatives on offer.

Berlin coalition talks have illustrated how fragile the mainstream bloc itself can be. Negotiations over Israel policy, antisemitism safeguards and the Gaza war collapsed before they could produce a working agreement, demonstrating that ideological divisions do not run only between mainstream parties and the AfD. From the left, critics argue that the coalition prioritises defence spending and business confidence over tenants, welfare recipients and public services, creating space for both far-right and far-left challengers.

Growth Forecasts Diverge From Kitchen-Table Reality

The German government has presented an upgraded economic outlook, forecasting GDP growth of 1.3 percent in 2026 and 1.1 percent in 2027, underpinned by planned infrastructure investment and faster structural reform. Officials argue that stronger-than-expected first-half performance and improving manufacturing conditions justify cautious optimism, and the coalition has described its economic programme as a response to a historic test for German democracy. Temporary fuel-tax reductions have been proposed to ease consumer pressure from rising energy costs.

The Bundesbank's published projections tell a more cautious story. One central bank forecast put growth at 0.7 percent for 2026, while another outlook cited figures of 0.5 percent for 2026 and 0.8 percent for 2027, well below the government's scenario. On inflation, the Bundesbank has warned that fuel prices, low gas inventories and refined oil products will keep price pressures elevated. It has also cautioned that healthcare reforms and changes to pharmacy rules could temporarily add close to half a percentage point to inflation in early 2027. Headline inflation reached 2.9 percent in August, remaining above the European Central Bank's 2 percent target.

Trade unions and opposition parties argue that these numbers do not capture what households are experiencing. Even if the inflation rate eventually moderates, the price level will not return to where it stood before the energy shock of recent years. A household that has absorbed higher heating bills, food costs and rents over two years does not recover that lost purchasing power when price rises simply slow. Critics also question whether temporary fuel-tax reductions address Germany's deeper structural problems, among them high energy costs, weak infrastructure, labour shortages and industrial uncertainty that have lingered well beyond the immediate post-pandemic period.

A Delivery Crisis With European Consequences

The most defensible reading of Germany's current situation is that mainstream parties face what analysts describe as a delivery crisis. The government's argument that visible reform, economic improvement and social cohesion can reduce support for the far right is logically coherent but as yet unproven. Approval ratings for the coalition remain historically weak, and there is no evidence in available data that the reform programme has yet reversed that trajectory. The government must demonstrate that democratic governance produces tangible results, not merely rhetorical opposition to the AfD.

For citizens, the practical consequences cover a wide range of daily concerns: the cost of heating and transport, job security in industrial sectors exposed to global competition, the quality of railways and schools, access to affordable housing and the reliability of public services. These are not abstract political questions. They are the conditions under which voters decide whether established institutions deserve their trust or whether alternatives, however radical, appear more responsive to their frustrations.

Germany's difficulties carry weight beyond its borders. Weak German demand reduces export revenues for suppliers across the EU single market, while persistent political uncertainty makes Berlin a less predictable partner on questions ranging from Ukraine policy and defence to climate targets and trade. A Germany that stabilises its politics and delivers on economic reform would strengthen European cohesion; one that remains mired in coalition infighting and populist pressure will be a source of turbulence for the bloc as a whole. The next months, as the coalition attempts to pass budgets, advance structural legislation and maintain the firewall under mounting parliamentary pressure, will test whether the gap between promised recovery and lived experience can be closed before voters lose patience entirely.
